subject: chemistry-2
question: Which comparison of a 0.1 M sodium chloride solution and a 0.1 M glucose solution is accurate with respect to dissolved particle concentration?

options.text: The NaCl solution is about 0.2 osmol/L because NaCl dissociates into two ions, while glucose stays as one particle
The glucose solution is about 0.2 osmol/L because each glucose molecule splits into two particles in water
Both are about 0.2 osmol/L because molarity already accounts for dissociation of the solute
Both are about 0.1 osmol/L because equal molarity means equal numbers of dissolved particles

explanation:
Sodium chloride is a strong electrolyte that dissociates essentially completely into Na+ and Cl-, so each mole yields approximately 2 osmoles and 0.1 M x 2 = 0.2 osmol/L. Glucose is a nonelectrolyte that dissolves as intact molecules, giving 0.1 osmol/L. Osmolarity rather than molarity governs osmotic pressure and the direction of water movement across a semipermeable membrane, which is why two equimolar solutions can behave very differently.

ELI-10: Molarity counts formula units before they dissolve; osmolarity counts the independent particles that exist afterward. Glucose dissolves intact, so one mole in gives one osmole of particles. NaCl separates into a sodium ion and a chloride ion, so one mole in gives about two osmoles. That is why the salt solution reaches 0.2 osmol/L at the same 0.1 M label. Osmosis responds to the number of dissolved particles rather than their identity or size, so the particle count is the figure that predicts water movement.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
